A system whose scores determine redundancy selection materially influences the outcome and fails the threshold test; and notwithstanding those conditions, a system that performs profiling of natural persons is always high-risk, which scoring individual employees on performance will ordinarily constitute. If you nonetheless conclude the system is not high-risk, Article 6(4) requires the provider to document that assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service, to register under Article 49(2), and to produce the documentation to national competent authorities on request.

No. Participation in the Spanish sandbox does not authorise placing the system on the market or putting it into service, so it cannot be commercially deployed to a real client while the sandbox phase is running: an AI regulatory sandbox is a controlled environment for the development, training, testing and validation of innovative AI systems for a limited time before their being placed on the market or put into service, pursuant to the specific sandbox plan agreed with the competent authority (Article 57(5)). What is available is real-world testing, not deployment. The sandbox itself may include testing in real world conditions supervised therein under the agreed sandbox plan (Article 57(5)), with the competent authority providing guidance, supervision and support to identify risks to fundamental rights, health and safety and to verify mitigation measures (Article 57(6)); the authority retains power to suspend the testing or the operator's participation where no effective mitigation is possible (Article 57(11)), and you remain liable for damage inflicted on third parties, although no administrative fines are imposed where you observe the sandbox plan and follow the authority's guidance in good faith (Article 57(12)). Alternatively, as a hiring system listed in Annex III, it may be tested in real world conditions outside the sandbox under Article 60, at any time before placing on the market or putting into service, on the operator's own or in partnership with one or more deployers or prospective deployers (Article 60(1)-(2)), that partnership, not a commercial contract, is the lawful way to involve the client. All of the following conditions must be met (Article 60(4)): a real-world testing plan drawn up and submitted to the market surveillance authority of the Member State of testing; approval by that authority of both the testing and the plan, with tacit approval after 30 days unless national law requires express authorisation; registration of the testing in accordance with Article 71(4) with a Union-wide unique single identification number and the information specified in Annex IX (the law-enforcement, migration, asylum and border-control systems of Annex III points 1, 6 and 7 registering instead in the secure non-public section under Article 49(4)(d), and Annex III point 2 systems under Article 49(5)); establishment in the Union or an appointed Union legal representative; transfer of collected data to third countries only with appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law; a testing duration no longer than necessary and in any event within the maximum period permitted, extendable only on notification; specific protection for subjects belonging to vulnerable groups by reason of age or disability; information to the cooperating deployers of all aspects of the testing relevant to their decision to participate; freely given informed consent of the subjects before participation; effective oversight by suitably qualified persons with the necessary capacity, training and authority; and predictions, recommendations or decisions that can be effectively reversed and disregarded. Testing is without prejudice to the prohibitions in Article 5 (Article 60(1)) and to any ethical review required by Union or national law (Article 60(3)). During such testing, subjects or their legally designated representatives may withdraw at any time without detriment or justification by revoking consent and may request immediate and permanent deletion of their personal data, without affecting activities already carried out (Article 60(5)); the market surveillance authority may require information, carry out unannounced remote or on-site inspections and check the conduct of the testing (Article 60(6)); any serious incident must be reported under Article 73, with immediate mitigation or suspension, termination and a prompt recall procedure (Article 60(7)); suspension, termination and final outcomes must be notified to that authority (Article 60(8)); and you remain liable for any damage caused in the course of the testing (Article 60(9)). Genuine deployment to the client may only follow completion of conformity assessment and CE marking and the system's placing on the market or putting into service.

No, the €35 000 000 figure is not the ceiling that applies to the operator. Article 99(3) does set the Article 5 ceiling at EUR 35 000 000 or 7 % of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher, but Article 99(6) reverses that arithmetic for SMEs, including start-ups: each fine under this Article is capped at the percentage or the fixed amount, whichever is lower. For a 25-person start-up, 7 % of worldwide annual turnover will be far below EUR 35 000 000, so 7 % of turnover is the operator's maximum exposure for the Article 5 breach. Two qualifiers narrow that relief. First, the cap keys to the undertaking's total worldwide annual turnover, so if the operator is part of a wider group the relevant turnover, and the operator's qualification as an SME, may be assessed at group level rather than by headcount alone. Second, the reduced ceiling is a maximum, not a discount on the assessment: under Article 99(1) penalties must still be effective, proportionate and dissuasive, and Article 99(7) requires the authority to weigh the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement and its consequences; whether other authorities have already fined the same operator for the same infringement; whether other authorities have already fined the operator for infringements of other Union or national law; the size, annual turnover and market share of the operator; any other aggravating or mitigating factor such as financial benefits gained or losses avoided; the degree of cooperation with national authorities; the operator's degree of responsibility, having regard to technical and organisational measures; how the infringement became known, in particular whether the operator notified it; the intentional or negligent character of the infringement; and any remedial action taken. The operator's knowing six-month deployment engages the duration and intentionality factors directly.

The Annex III route, classification under Article 6(2), not the Annex I product route under Article 6(1). Article 6(1) applies only where the AI system is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation; an employment system reaches high-risk status instead because it is an AI system referred to in Annex III, which Article 6(2) deems high-risk in addition to those under paragraph 1. Being "under Annex III(4)" is not by itself decisive: the numbered heading is an area, and only a listed lettered use-case triggers Article 6(2). Annex III(4) contains two: point (a), AI systems intended to be used for the recruitment or selection of natural persons, in particular to place targeted job advertisements, to analyse and filter job applications, and to evaluate candidates; and point (b), AI systems intended to be used to make decisions affecting terms of work-related relationships, the promotion or termination of work-related contractual relationships, to allocate tasks based on individual behaviour or personal traits or characteristics, or to monitor and evaluate the performance and behaviour of persons in such relationships. Confirm the system's intended purpose maps onto (a) or (b). If it does, the only exit is the Article 6(3) derogation: the system is not high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety or fundamental rights of natural persons, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making, and one of four conditions is met, (a) it performs a narrow procedural task; (b) it improves the result of a previously completed human activity; (c) it detects decision-making patterns or deviations from prior decision-making patterns and is not meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment, without proper human review; or (d) it performs a preparatory task to an assessment relevant for the Annex III use cases. Notwithstanding those conditions, the system is always high-risk where it performs profiling of natural persons, a common outcome in candidate scoring and worker-behaviour analytics, which would close the derogation off. A provider relying on Article 6(3) must, under Article 6(4), document that assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service, is subject to the registration obligation in Article 49(2), and must provide the documentation to national competent authorities on request.

Annex I embedded high-risk obligations apply from 2 August 2027, one year later than the general application date. Under Article 113(2) the Regulation applies from 2 August 2026, but Article 113(3)(c) defers Article 6(1) and the corresponding obligations in the Regulation to 2 August 2027, giving the extra transition to AI that rides inside regulated products. (This is the date in Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 as adopted; it is not affected by the later political agreement referred to for the Annex III route.). That deferral attaches only where both limbs of the Article 6(1) product route are met: the AI system is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation for placing on the market or putting into service. For medical devices this means Regulation (EU) 2017/745 (Annex I, point 11) and, for in vitro diagnostics, Regulation (EU) 2017/746 (Annex I, point 12), alongside the other Annex I acts such as machinery, toys, lifts, radio equipment, pressure equipment, PPE and the Section B transport acts. Two qualifiers. The Article 6(3) derogation is available only for Annex III systems and cannot be used to escape the Annex I product route. And the deferral is confined to Article 6(1) and its corresponding obligations, the Article 5 prohibitions still bind from 2 February 2025 and the Article 4 AI-literacy duty from the same date, irrespective of the product's classification, so an embedded medical-device AI must be Article 5-compliant well before its high-risk obligations bite.

No, not in this version. The text the operator is working from is Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 as adopted, and the Digital Omnibus is a subsequent Commission legislative initiative that sits outside that corpus; it has not altered a single date in the adopted Regulation, so the transitional deadlines stand exactly as enacted and any deferral it may propose cannot be read into this version. On the adopted text, the relevant dates remain those in Article 111: AI systems that are components of the large-scale IT systems established by the acts listed in Annex X and placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2027 must be brought into compliance by 31 December 2030, with the Regulation's requirements taken into account in the evaluations of those systems foreseen in the Annex X acts and where those acts are replaced or amended (Article 111(1)); that carve-out is expressly without prejudice to the application of Article 5, which applies on its own earlier date. High-risk AI systems other than those Annex X components, placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2026, are caught only if their design is significantly changed thereafter, save that systems intended for use by public authorities must in any event be brought into compliance by 2 August 2030 (Article 111(2)). Providers of general-purpose AI models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 must take the necessary steps to comply by 2 August 2027 (Article 111(3)). If you need an assessment of what a later amending instrument would do to those dates, that requires the amended consolidated text rather than the as-adopted version supplied here.

Not adhering to the Code of Practice is permissible; it simply shifts you onto a self-evidencing route. Article 53(4) sets out two alternatives to reliance on an Article 56 code for the Article 53(1) obligations (Annex XI technical documentation, Annex XII downstream-provider information, the copyright policy and the public training-data summary). First, you may comply with a European harmonised standard: compliance with such standards grants a presumption of conformity, but only to the extent that those standards cover those obligations, so any obligation left uncovered still has to be evidenced separately. Second, and this is the residual path where no harmonised standard has been published or you choose not to apply one, a provider that neither adheres to an approved code of practice nor complies with a European harmonised standard "shall demonstrate alternative adequate means of compliance for assessment by the Commission" (Article 53(4)). That is a substantive obligation, not a passive option: the burden is on you to document and present the operator's own compliance means, and they are assessed by the Commission rather than self-certified. Reliance on a code is in any event transitional, it is available "until a harmonised standard is published.". If the operator's model is classified as having systemic risk under Article 51(1) (presumed where cumulative training compute exceeds 10²⁵ floating-point operations, Article 51(2)), the identical structure applies a second time to the Article 55(1) obligations, model evaluation including adversarial testing, assessment and mitigation of Union-level systemic risks, serious-incident tracking, documentation and reporting to the AI Office, and cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure, with the same three options and the same fallback duty to demonstrate alternative adequate means of compliance for assessment by the Commission (Article 55(2)). Two qualifiers bear on the practical exposure. Information and documentation you hand over, including trade secrets, is protected by the confidentiality regime of Article 78 (Articles 53(7) and 55(3)). And the alternative-means route is not a permanent free-standing regime: under Article 56(9), if a code of practice cannot be finalised by 2 August 2025 or the AI Office assesses it as inadequate under Article 56(6), the Commission may lay down common rules for the implementation of Articles 53 and 55 by implementing act, which would then bind you irrespective of the operator's non-adherence. Note also that adherence, where offered, may be partial: Article 56(7) allows providers of models not presenting systemic risks to limit adherence to the Article 53 obligations unless they explicitly declare an interest in joining the full code.

No. Article 88 is not a fining provision, and the AI Office is not itself the fining authority. Article 88(1) does two things only: it vests in the Commission the exclusive powers to supervise and enforce Chapter V, subject to the procedural guarantees of Article 94, and it requires the Commission to entrust the implementation of those tasks to the AI Office, without prejudice to the Commission's powers of internal organisation and to the division of competences between the Member States and the Union under the Treaties (Article 88(1)). Article 88(2) adds only that, without prejudice to Article 75(3), market surveillance authorities may request the Commission to exercise those powers where necessary and proportionate to assist them with their tasks. The power to fine a provider of a general-purpose AI model rests instead with the Commission under Article 101(1), which allows fines not exceeding 3 % of the provider's annual total worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year or EUR 15 000 000, whichever is higher, where the Commission finds that the provider acted intentionally or negligently in that it: (a) infringed the relevant provisions of the Regulation; (b) failed to comply with a request for a document or information pursuant to Article 91, or supplied incorrect, incomplete or misleading information; (c) failed to comply with a measure requested under Article 93; or (d) failed to make available to the Commission access to the general-purpose AI model, or the general-purpose AI model with systemic risk, for an evaluation pursuant to Article 92. In fixing the amount, regard must be had to the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement and to proportionality and appropriateness, and account must also be taken of commitments made under Article 93(3) or in codes of practice under Article 56 (Article 101(1)). The formal act is therefore a Commission decision, not an AI Office decision: the AI Office conducts the supervision, investigation and enforcement preparation as the Commission's delegated implementer under Article 88(1), while the fining decision is adopted by the Commission under Article 101, after the provider has been given the opportunity to be heard (Article 101(2)), with the fine subject to the review of the Court of Justice of the European Union, which has unlimited jurisdiction to cancel, reduce or increase it (Article 101(5)). National market surveillance authorities have no parallel fining power over providers of general-purpose AI models in respect of Chapter V, because that enforcement competence is exclusive to the Commission (Article 88(1)); their Article 74 powers attach to AI systems within their competence, with cooperation channelled through Article 88(2).

No retrofit is required: a high‑risk AI system placed on the market in March 2026 is grandfathered, and the provider must bring it into conformity only if, as from 2 August 2026, the system is subject to significant changes in its design. The operative rule is Article 111(2): this Regulation applies to operators of high‑risk AI systems, other than those referred to in Article 111(1), that were placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2026 only if, as from that date, those systems are subject to significant changes in their designs. A March 2026 placing therefore falls on the protected side of the cut‑off, and the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements together with the Article 43 conformity‑assessment and CE‑marking obligations are not triggered retroactively. The transitional wording is not limited to one classification route, so it covers both an Annex III listed‑use system under Article 6(2) and an Annex I safety‑component/product system under Article 6(1). Four qualifications complete the rule. First, the grandfathering is expressly without prejudice to Article 5 as referred to in Article 113(3), point (a), the prohibitions bite irrespective of the placing date. Second, it does not cover the systems in Article 111(1): AI systems that are components of the large‑scale IT systems established by the acts listed in Annex X and placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2027 must instead be brought into compliance by 31 December 2030. Third, a backstop applies regardless of design changes: providers and deployers of high‑risk AI systems intended to be used by public authorities shall take the necessary steps to comply by 2 August 2030 (Article 111(2), second sentence). Fourth, once a significant design change occurs, the full regime, including conformity assessment, applies prospectively: for Annex III point 1 systems, Article 43(1) offers internal control under Annex VI where harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied, and the Annex VII notified‑body route where the provider has not applied them, applied only part of a harmonised standard, has not applied existing common specifications, or a standard was published with a restriction; for Annex III points 2 to 8, Annex VI internal control applies (Article 43(2)); for Annex I‑covered products, the assessment is integrated into the sectoral third‑party procedure (Article 43(3)). Note also that Article 43(4) independently requires a new conformity assessment on substantial modification of a system that has already undergone one, with pre‑determined changes documented under point 2(f) of Annex IV not counting as such.In practice, then, the March 2026 system may continue to be made available as it stands, but the provider should keep the documentation supporting that dating and treat any significant change in design as from 2 August 2026 as the point at which full compliance, including the applicable Article 43 procedure and CE marking, becomes due.

The customer has an enforceable right to an explanation from you as deployer, and the operator must provide it. Because the operator's system evaluates the creditworthiness of natural persons, it is a high-risk AI system under Annex III(5)(b) via Article 6(2), and it is not a system listed under point 2 of Annex III (critical infrastructure), so the carve-out in Article 86(1) does not apply. A loan denial is a decision taken by the deployer on the basis of the system's output that produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects the applicant in a way they consider to have an adverse impact on their fundamental rights, which triggers Article 86(1). What you owe is clear and meaningful explanations of two things: the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure, that is, whether the output was determinative, advisory or one input among several, and how it fed into the final denial, and the main elements of the decision taken, meaning the principal factors and reasoning that produced the rejection, not merely a statement that a model was used (Article 86(1)). Two limits qualify the duty. First, the right does not apply to the use of AI systems for which exceptions from, or restrictions to, that obligation follow from Union or national law in compliance with Union law (Article 86(2)); in lending this typically covers matters such as statutory anti-money-laundering or fraud-related restrictions, and the operator should identify the specific legal basis before withholding any element rather than relying on a general commercial-confidentiality claim. Second, Article 86 applies only to the extent that the right is not otherwise provided for under Union law (Article 86(3)), so where the applicant's explanation right is already covered by another Union instrument, that instrument governs; Article 86 complements rather than displaces the data-protection framework and does not reduce what is owed there. Note also that if the operator's system were merely performing a narrow procedural or preparatory task under the Article 6(3) derogation it would fall outside the high-risk classification, but a system making loan denials that profiles natural persons is always high-risk under the final subparagraph of Article 6(3), so that route is closed here.

A separate person established in the Union must take that role: because the US parent is a provider established in a third country, Article 22(1) obliges it, prior to making its high-risk AI system available on the Union market, to appoint by written mandate an authorised representative established in the Union. The absence of any EU establishment is precisely the trigger for that duty, not an excuse from it; the mandate-holder may be any natural or legal person established in a Member State (for example an EU group affiliate, or a contracted third-party representation service), provided it is empowered to perform the mandated tasks, and the US parent must enable it to do so under Article 22(2). The mandate must cover the full set of tasks in Article 22(3): verifying that the EU declaration of conformity and the technical documentation have been drawn up and that an appropriate conformity assessment procedure has been carried out by the provider (point (a)); keeping at the disposal of the competent authorities and national authorities, for 10 years after the system has been placed on the market or put into service, the provider's contact details, a copy of the EU declaration of conformity, the technical documentation and, where applicable, the certificate issued by the notified body (point (b)); providing a competent authority, upon a reasoned request, with all the information and documentation necessary to demonstrate conformity, including access to the automatically generated logs to the extent those are under the provider's control (point (c)); cooperating with competent authorities, upon a reasoned request, on any action taken in relation to the high-risk AI system, in particular to reduce and mitigate the risks it poses (point (d)); and, where applicable, complying with the registration obligations in Article 49(1), or, where the provider registers itself, ensuring that the information referred to in point 3 of Section A of Annex VIII is correct (point (e)). The mandate must further empower the authorised representative to be addressed, in addition to or instead of the provider, by the competent authorities on all issues related to ensuring compliance with the Regulation. The role is a representation function, not a transfer of provider status: the US parent remains bound by the substantive requirements, including the risk management system (Article 9), data governance (Article 10), technical documentation (Article 11 and Annex IV), logging (Article 12), transparency and instructions for use (Article 13), conformity assessment (Article 43), the EU declaration of conformity (Article 47), CE marking (Article 48), post-market monitoring (Article 72) and serious-incident reporting (Article 73). The representative's identity and contact details must appear in the instructions for use under Article 13(3)(a) and in the EU declaration of conformity per Annex V, and registration in the EU database under Article 49(1), or under Article 49(2) for a system the provider has concluded is not high-risk pursuant to Article 6(3), is made by the provider or, where applicable, the authorised representative. Finally, Article 22(4) imposes an independent safeguard: the authorised representative must terminate the mandate if it considers, or has reason to consider, that the provider is acting contrary to its obligations under the Regulation, and must in that case immediately inform the relevant market surveillance authority and, where applicable, the relevant notified body of the termination and its reasons.
